title: Fourier Transform: seeing the rotating ingredients inside a signal
bigIdea: Any repeating-looking signal can be understood as a mixture of simple rotating motions, and the Fourier transform reveals how much of each frequency is present so that filtering and convolution become visible operations.

concepts.title: Rotating vectors can draw shapes
concepts.summary: The tip of one rotating arrow traces a circle; a chain of rotating arrows added end to end can trace surprisingly rich closed paths.
concepts.intuition: A rotating arrow is a tiny motion recipe, and a chain of recipes can add up to a drawing.
misconceptions: One rotating vector can draw any shape by itself.
The circles are the final picture rather than scaffolding for the moving tip.
Adding more circles always makes the drawing exact.
visualHooks: Nested bicycle wheels whose axle tips trace a heart.
Orbiting planets hand a pen from one center to the next.
A spinning arrow leaves a bright trail only at its endpoint.

concepts.title: Complex numbers are points with a built-in turn
concepts.summary: A complex number a+bi names a point in the plane, while multiplying by a unit complex number changes its angle and rotates it without changing its length.
concepts.intuition: Complex multiplication is geometry in disguise: length scales and angles add.
misconceptions: The symbol i is an ordinary real number with a negative value.
A complex number is two unrelated numbers rather than one geometric point.
Multiplying by i makes a vector longer because it adds a dimension.
visualHooks: A coordinate plane where i is a quarter-turn button.
Two arrows multiply by composing their stretches and rotations.
A compass needle turning as e^{iθ} is dialed.

concepts.title: A rotating vector is a complex exponential
concepts.summary: The expression e^{iωt} is a unit vector rotating at angular speed ω; multiplying it by a complex coefficient sets a component's size and starting phase.
concepts.intuition: One complex exponential is a clock hand whose speed, length, and starting angle are all explicit.
misconceptions: The imaginary exponent makes the value grow exponentially in magnitude.
Changing phase changes frequency.
A negative frequency means a negative physical time.
visualHooks: A clock hand labelled ωt sweeping around the unit circle.
A coefficient arrow attached to a faster or slower rotor.
Clockwise and counterclockwise hands for opposite signed frequencies.

concepts.title: Sinusoids are shadows of rotation
concepts.summary: Projecting uniform circular motion onto one axis produces a sine or cosine wave; amplitude controls the excursion and frequency controls how quickly cycles repeat.
concepts.intuition: A sine wave is what a steady circular motion looks like when seen edge-on.
misconceptions: Amplitude changes how often the wave cycles.
A phase shift changes the wave's frequency.
Sine and cosine are fundamentally different kinds of motion.
visualHooks: A bead moving around a circle casts a moving shadow on a wall.
The same rotor shown from above and then edge-on.
A stretched and compressed wave beside its circular source.

concepts.title: Frequency is the pace of repetition
concepts.summary: Frequency counts cycles per unit time, while angular frequency is 2π times that rate; high frequency means faster oscillation, not necessarily larger amplitude.
concepts.intuition: Frequency is the tempo of a repeating motion; amplitude is how far the motion reaches.
misconceptions: A higher frequency must have a higher amplitude.
Frequency and period both measure the same number with the same units.
A signal has only one frequency because it has one time axis.
visualHooks: Slow and fast metronomes tracing waves with equal height.
A race between a short-period and long-period oscillator.
A frequency dial that changes spacing while leaving height fixed.

concepts.title: Correlating with a sinusoid measures its ingredient
concepts.summary: Multiplying a signal by a reference sinusoid and averaging over a whole number of cycles measures how strongly that frequency is present.
concepts.intuition: An inner product is a detector tuned to one pattern: it reports how much the signal points in that direction.
misconceptions: The average of a product is always zero for oscillating signals.
Correlation with a frequency proves the signal contains only that frequency.
The detector works the same way if the observation window cuts a cycle in half.
visualHooks: A lock-in amplifier turning a knob until two waves line up.
Positive and negative lobes cancelling except for the matching rhythm.
A projection shadow growing when the reference wave matches.

concepts.title: Different frequencies can be perpendicular
concepts.summary: Over a complete shared period, distinct integer-frequency sines and cosines have zero inner product, so their coefficients can be measured independently.
concepts.intuition: Orthogonality makes different rhythms invisible to one another when averaged over the right interval.
misconceptions: Perpendicular only makes sense for arrows drawn in two dimensions.
Any two different frequencies cancel on every interval.
Zero inner product means both signals are zero.
visualHooks: Two waves whose product has equal positive and negative area.
A high-dimensional coordinate grid with sine waves as axes.
A rotating projection landing at the origin after a full period.

concepts.title: Fourier series rebuild periodic signals
concepts.summary: A periodic function can be represented as a constant plus weighted sine and cosine harmonics; orthogonality supplies each weight by projection.
concepts.intuition: A Fourier series is a recipe that stacks simple pure tones until their sum matches a repeating shape.
misconceptions: A Fourier series uses only one sine wave.
The sharp corners of a square wave mean the series has stopped converging.
The coefficients are arbitrary knobs rather than measured projections.
visualHooks: Harmonic circles assembling a square wave one layer at a time.
A mixing desk with fundamental and integer overtones.
A smooth approximation tightening around a jump as terms are added.

concepts.title: The Fourier transform scans a continuum of frequencies
concepts.summary: For a nonperiodic signal, the Fourier transform records its correlation with every continuous frequency, turning a time description into a frequency description.
concepts.intuition: The transform is a bank of infinitely many rhythm detectors, one for each possible frequency.
misconceptions: The transform throws away time and therefore cannot describe transient signals.
A frequency spectrum is always a list of separate spikes.
The transform and its inverse are the same operation with no convention choices.
visualHooks: A spotlight sweeping across a continuous frequency ruler.
A burst in time spreading into a broad spectrum.
Two views of the same signal linked by a rotating detector bank.

concepts.title: Convolution filters by multiplying spectra
concepts.summary: Convolution combines a signal with a response kernel in time; the convolution theorem says this becomes pointwise multiplication in frequency, making filtering transparent.
concepts.intuition: A filter keeps, weakens, or delays frequency ingredients, and convolution is the time-domain way those choices act on a signal.
misconceptions: Convolution is ordinary multiplication at matching time points.
A low-pass filter removes all detail rather than selectively reducing rapid variation.
Multiplication in one domain always means convolution in the same domain.
visualHooks: A sliding kernel brushing across a signal and accumulating weighted overlap.
A frequency gate dimming fast rotors while passing slow ones.
The same filter shown as a blur in time and a mask in frequency.
